The NV-1 chip includes 3200 cores per chip with seamless I/O compatibility to increase array size via chaining chips.
During testing, the NV-1 chip achieved 447 GB/s per 0.25 W, demonstrating both high performance and radical power-use improvement over other comparable hardware devices.
The NV-1 chip has been successfully fielded in a real-world edge sensor application, performing real-time processing with a power budget of less than 10 mW.
The co-design process used a digital twin approach, developing a C++ software executable hardware model from the beginning to enable closed-loop communication between the hardware and software teams.
The NV architecture was designed from first principles to eliminate almost all memory bandwidth bottlenecks, a major throughput and efficiency limitation in CPUs and GPUs.
The NV-1 chip does not use caches or a global memory space, unlike GPUs which extensively use caches to minimize their memory bottlenecks.
The NV-1 chip achieved a best-case adjusted efficiency of 1352 TOPS/W for boolean arithmetic, orders of magnitude higher than other edge AI processors.
The NV platform is targeted at low-power, high-performance edge devices and internet-of-things applications, as well as massively parallel server farm applications.
The teams are working on the next version, NV-2, which will further improve on power usage and minimize the physical size of each core through resource sharing.
The communication protocol of the NV platform enables scaling up to huge arrays of NV chiplets for applications requiring massive parallelism.
The NV-1 chip has been successfully manufactured in 28nm TSMC technology, received in packaged dies, and functionally characterized and verified.
The NV architecture derives from operations of extremely large numbers of simple parallel elements in complex arrangements, inspired by the brain's circuitry.
The co-design approach allowed the hardware to be specifically developed to accelerate the parallel algorithms and software, without the need for compromises.
The NV-1 chip has been tested in real-world settings, performing real-time processing of a chemical sensor with a power budget of less than 10 mW.
The NV-1 chip achieved a peak memory bandwidth of 447 GB/s per 0.25 W of power, orders of magnitude higher than the memory bandwidth of other AI accelerators.
